feedback: If a mark lands on the wrong fractional interval (e.g. at 3/8 when the value is 1/2 = 4/8), point to a labelled position and count the eighths across to re-place it; the plot's structure is fine, only the placement slipped.
If observed values are drawn as adjacent bars with no empty positions between them, show a ruler: every eighth exists on the scale, so unobserved positions must stay visible as gaps.
If fractions are added by combining numerators and denominators (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/6), re-label both in eighths first (4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8) and check the sum against the scale.

If the fair share is answered with an unchanged amount, or by picking a middle or most common value without working, pour everything together to get the total, then share it among all the containers: equally means total ÷ count. (For 3/4, 1/2, 1/4, 1/2 the middle value happens to equal the fair share of 1/2, so ask to see the total-and-divide working rather than judging by the answer alone.)
activities.intendedInsight: A line plot's axis is a continuous measurement scale with gaps for unobserved values, not a row of categories; and 'share the total equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share, which previews the mean made physical.
learnerActions: Measure (or use given) several lengths to the nearest 1/8 and place a mark (an X or dot) above each value on a horizontal scale marked in eighths.
Keep every eighth-position on the scale visible, including positions where no measurement falls, so the gaps are shown (for example, if nothing lands on 4 5/8, that spot stays on the number line).
Say aloud why an unobserved value still has a place on the scale: it is a measurement value on a ruler-like scale, not a separate category.

For a fair-share task, start with four identical (same-size) containers holding 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/2 cup. Combine all the liquid into one larger container that can hold at least 2 cups, and write the sum, re-labelling each amount in eighths: 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups.
Pour the combined 2 cups equally back into the four identical containers and record how much each now holds; connect the result (1/2 cup each) to total ÷ count = 2 ÷ 4.
Total the two shortest measurements and find a difference between two values, re-expressing over a common denominator first.
activities.title: Place-and-share: build the plot, then pour the total

feedback: For an answer that adds tops and bottoms (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 giving 4/6), re-express both in eighths and recompute; 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8.
For a fair-share answer that is the most common amount or an unchanged value, re-total all amounts and divide by the number of containers.
If a difference is found without first making like denominators, re-express both values in eighths before subtracting, then check the result against the scale.
activities.intendedInsight: Totals, differences and fair shares read off a line plot all depend on correct like-denominator fraction arithmetic and on reading 'equally' as total ÷ count.
learnerActions: From a provided small line plot, write the total of the two shortest measurements, showing the common-denominator step.
Answer a fair-share question such as 'If all the liquid were shared equally between identical containers, how much would each hold?' by totalling then dividing by the count.
Compare two values to find a difference, re-expressing over eighths first.
Watch for and avoid two traps: adding numerators and denominators together, and reporting a middle value instead of total ÷ count.
activities.title: Check the operations on a given plot

feedback: If the learner says the empty spot should be removed, return to the ruler image: a measurement value is not a category, so its position exists regardless of whether data falls there.

If adding the zero container does not change the learner's answer, recompute total ÷ count with the new count (2 cups ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each): the fair share is sensitive to how many are sharing, even when the added amount is zero.
If the fruit bar chart and the line plot are treated as the same, point out that fruit names are categories with no scale, while lengths sit on a measurement number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why unobserved positions remain on the scale, why common denominators are needed, and how the fair share responds to the count (including a zero) consolidates both the display and the averaging ideas.
learnerActions: Answer: 'You didn't measure any item at 4 5/8 — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' to put the measurement-scale-vs-category distinction into words.
Explain why you changed both fractions into eighths before adding them.
Tackle a counterexample: 'If one more identical container with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' and state why the answer changes.
Contrast this line plot with a bar chart of favourite fruits and say what makes the axes different.
activities.title: Explain and stretch the fair-share idea
